name: Beth Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play flute for a chamber trio, record short breathing exercises for students and coach two adult players. My music degree and twenty-three years on stage help me settle a shaky entrance, but most of my work is booked one date at a time. I like the moment a learner can hold one clean phrase.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that calendar mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner works variable hours at a print shop, and our children are grown. We rent, have two weeks of expenses saved, and my pay sits below most experienced players'. There are few other flute jobs within our bus route. I use AI daily to draft rehearsal lists, then check every name and date on the signed sheet.

say: I'd welcome **quicker lists** with written fees and rehearsal rooms.
I'd say a **student's phrase** still needs a player breathing with it.
think: Our **two-week reserve** cannot absorb a missed trio date.
My partner's **variable print hours** leave the rent exposed.
do: Confirm **five paid dates** and two pupils; request written cancellation fees this week.
Check **AI list drafts** against the signed hall sheet and save thirty only from an extra cleared fee after essentials.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary contract gaps reaching rent.
S0.quote: I want a written call, not a family loan disguised as music pay.
fieldNote: Her **low experienced pay** and two-week reserve make even ordinary cancelled concert dates dangerous for rent.
Daily **AI list drafting** is existing use, checked against the hall's signed sheet.

steps.text: Confirm five paid trio dates and two pupils; request written cancellation fees
Check AI lists against signed sheet; save thirty from extra cleared fee after rent/food/flute repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the trio that a quicker list is useful if the fee and rehearsal room are still written beside each name. A computer cannot breathe the phrase for the student.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missed trio date already threatens our rent because two weeks is all we have saved. My partner's print hours change, so mild AI leaves the old contract problem in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm five paid trio dates and my two pupils, and ask the booker for written cancellation fees. In the first year of this mild change I'll continue checking my daily AI list drafts against the signed hall sheet; if an extra paid concert clears after rent, food and flute repairs, I'll save thirty from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a cancelled call even if AI stays small. Two weeks of money is not enough for a quiet month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after a cancelled show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A storm cancelled one outdoor show in June after we had paid for the bus. The booker had never put a cancellation fee in the contract, so we lost the whole date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children help with a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the children have their own bills. I want a written call, not a family loan disguised as music pay.

say: I'd ask which **paid breathing tracks** software might replace.
I'd seek **written rates** for recordings and rehearsals before another term.
think: Tracks bring **nearly one third** of my own pay.
Our **two-week reserve** and few local jobs cannot support a long search.
do: Compare **eight invoices** with new orders and request a paid lesson outside booked trio calls.
Test **AI cleaner** after paid lesson only on owned nameless audio with centre-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage.
Compare **cleaned audio** by ear; stop wrong notes or leakage and require written learner consent before other recordings.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic losses to my own track income.
S1.quote: A cleaner flute breathing-track file does not create a buyer.
fieldNote: The **new tool** differs from her daily list drafts and needs paid instruction outside paid trio time.
The **test audio** is owned, nameless, commercially licensed and stored locally with manual stop checks.

steps.text: Compare eight track invoices and request paid cleaner lesson outside booked trio calls
Test cleaner after paid lesson: owned nameless audio, funded paid-use licence and approved local storage
Compare audio by ear; stop wrong notes or leaks; require consent for learner recordings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the music centre which paid breathing-track orders its new software will replace. I would ask for the revised recording and rehearsal rates in writing before agreeing to another term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Breathing tracks bring almost a third of my pay. If the centre buys fewer, our two-week reserve and thin local job list will make a long search impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare my last eight track invoices with the centre's new orders and ask for a paid lesson on its new AI audio cleaner, which removes background hiss. In the first year I'll test only a nameless recording I own if the centre funds a licence permitting paid use and approves local storage; I'll listen beside the original and stop if it changes a note or sends the file outside the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing track fees while still needing to pay rent. I like learning a useful tool. A cleaner flute breathing-track file does not create a buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the lesson displace a paid trio date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid lesson must fit around, not replace, a booked trio call. If the centre won't pay for the hour and licence, I'll use my original audio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a student's recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't put a student's breath or name into the test. A learner's recording would need written consent and a storage rule before any use.

I'd ask for **written live dates** while venues still book the trio.
think: I expect **nearly one-third pay** from tracks to end in 2028.
Further **live-date cuts** remain possible rather than certain.
do: Count **track income**, request signed trio dates and an actual pension estimate before stopping work.
Seek **posted school work** after 2028 live cuts only if degree/experience qualify, written net after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit.
Keep **trio calls and pupils** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected track loss against two weeks saved.
S2.quote: Turning 60 cannot replace a written estimate of what would actually be paid.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 track loss** comes before 2031 flute-playing robots.
A school move needs **posted qualification**, written replacement net after travel, workable bus and signed offer.

steps.text: Count tracks, request signed paid trio dates and actual pension estimate before stopping
Seek posted school tutor job after live cuts if music degree and teaching qualify
Require written net after travel replacing losses and workable buses for school shifts
Keep paid trio calls and pupils until suitable signed school offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the trio that thinking AGI by 2028 could make breathing tracks before a robot can play flute. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I want live dates in writing while venues still book us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect track orders to stop in 2028 and take nearly a third of my pay. Live trio dates might also fall, but that is a second risk, not a fee I have lost yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total track income, ask for signed paid trio dates and request an actual pension estimate before considering any stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live dates also fall, I'll seek a posted paid school music-tutor job only if my music degree and adult teaching qualify, the written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses run at shift end; I'll keep trio calls and pupils until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by an expected loss of nearly a third of my pay with only two weeks saved. A local posting would help, but I cannot claim one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that school job open today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have seen only last year's school notice. I'll read a current paid posting with hours before I put a tutor wage into our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have no pension figure in hand. Turning 60 cannot replace a written estimate of what would actually be paid.

say: I'd price a **separate flute circle** before inviting anyone.
I'd require a **written room fee** before taking places.
think: A paper list of names cannot cover **room or preparation** costs.
do: Offer **four-week flute circle** after signed room/insurance and six fees cover hire, insurance, cleaning, inspected flutes, my teaching/preparation and bus.
Inspect **loan flutes** and personal head joints; defer and refund everyone if fewer than six safe paid places remain.
Renew **after 2031** with six safe fees covering room/insurance/cleaning/safe-hire/inspection/teaching/preparation/bus and written terms; keep booked trio/pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** until actual fees cover the whole class.
S3.quote: Our rent account cannot be the flute circle's hall-hire safety net.
fieldNote: The **six-place floor** pays her teaching/preparation/travel, room/insurance/cleaning and safe flute hire including technician inspection.
An **unsafe flute** reduces safe enrollment unless repaired or replaced; otherwise all deposits are refunded.

steps.text: Offer circle after signed room/insurance and six fees cover hire/insurance/safety/cleaning/teaching/preparation/bus
Inspect loan flutes and head joints; defer and refund whole group below six safe paid places
Renew after 2031 with six safe fees covering room/insurance/cleaning/safe-hire/inspection/teaching/preparation/bus under written terms
Keep booked paid trio dates and existing pupils while testing separate circle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the arts centre that five years to AGI by 2031 gives us time to price a separate live flute circle. Robots playing flutes follow around 2034; I would not invite anyone until the room fee is written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software might make my tracks cheaper before 2031. I can teach a first lesson, but a full room on paper will not pay for the hall or my preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll ask the centre for signed room, hire and insurance terms before taking fees for a separate four-week adult flute circle. Six adults must prepay enough for room, insurance, cleaning, sound loan flutes with technician inspection included, my teaching, preparation and bus fares; a technician must inspect the loan instruments and each learner needs a personal head joint, the mouthpiece section of the flute. In the first year after 2031 I'll renew only if six safe paid places cover those same costs and written room terms remain; if fewer safe places remain, I'll defer and refund the whole group, while keeping booked trio dates and pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious until six real fees cover the circle. Our rent account cannot be the flute circle's hall-hire safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a loan flute is unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If one loan flute cannot be cleaned or repaired, I would ask that learner to bring a sound instrument. If six safe paid places still cannot be made, I'd refund everyone before the first class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for your preparation and travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The six fees must cover my teaching hour, my setup time and the bus, not just the room. I can prepare the scores myself because I have taught adults for years.

I'd tell my children **2039 flute robots** do not change our monthly rent date.
think: At **68**, I may still need trio and teaching fees.
Our **two-week reserve** and unknown pension cannot fund a stopping date.
do: Request **actual pension estimate** and two-year paid-call plan; save 10% of extra cleared concerts after rent/food/repairs toward two months.
Keep **paid calls and pupils** after 2036; slow only if actual pension and paid fees cover bills.
Renew **flute circle** after 2036 only with six safe fees covering room/insurance/cleaning/safe-hire/inspection/teaching/preparation/bus under written terms; otherwise defer and refund everyone.
feel: I feel **anxious** about long-term income with little saved.
S4.quote: The longer warning gives me time to check a number, not the money itself.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and two-year written paid-call plan before reducing work
Save 10% of extra cleared concert fees after rent/food/flute repairs toward two months
Keep paid trio calls/pupils after 2036; slow only if pension and fees cover bills
Renew circle after 2036 with six safe fees covering room/insurance/cleaning/safe-hire/inspection/teaching/preparation/bus under written terms; otherwise defer/refund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children that ten years to thinking AGI by 2036 gives us time to check retirement income and written music calls. Flute-playing robots follow around 2039, but our rent has a date every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still need trio and teaching fees. Two weeks saved today and an unknown pension are not grounds for saying I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request an actual pension estimate and ask the trio for a written two-year paid-call plan. I'll put ten percent of each extra cleared paid concert fee into savings after rent, food and instrument repairs toward two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid calls and pupils while booked, and continue the separate flute circle only if six safe prepaid places still cover room, insurance, cleaning, inspected safe flute hire, my teaching, preparation and bus under written room terms; if not, I'll defer and refund everyone, reducing paid work only if actual pension and fees cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about reaching 68 with so little saved. The longer warning gives me time to check a number, not the money itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra concert pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra concert pays, nothing from that source goes into savings. I won't make the target by moving food money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen a pension statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't seen a pension statement yet. I would decide whether to slow down only after reading the actual amount with my partner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because track fees could disappear before another paid role appears. Signed trio dates, a real pension estimate and a posted qualifying school job with written replacement net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the bus fare when a flute class moves halls. A full register is not a wage if the journey and my preparation are unpaid.

headlineQuote: A full register is not a wage if the journey and my preparation are unpaid.
portrait: Beth is a **58-year-old experienced flutist** with a music degree, partner and grown children.
Her **low pay**, two-week reserve and few nearby jobs make lost track orders hard to replace.
She uses **AI daily** for lists and learns new audio cleanup only with paid instruction and private licensed trials.
She tests a **separate flute circle** only when six safe paid places cover room, her full work and travel.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase nearly a third of Beth's own pay from breathing tracks.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed trio dates**, a real pension estimate and posted qualifying school work with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
